At 3:17 in the morning, the city’s traffic lights continued their patient work for no one.

Red held the empty avenue. Green released it. Yellow cautioned the rain.

Mara watched from the laundromat across the street, sitting on a molded plastic chair with a book open in her lap. She hadn’t turned a page in twenty minutes. The dryers hummed behind her, each round window flashing shirts, towels, and pale sheets like weather systems on distant planets.

Her father’s coat was in the washer.

It was the only thing she had taken from his apartment after he died. Everything else had been practical: papers to the lawyer, dishes to the charity shop, medicine to the pharmacy, keys to the landlord. Her brother had wanted the radio, an old wooden thing that received only one station clearly. Mara had let him have it.

But the coat she kept.

It smelled of cigarettes, cedar, and the peppermint candies he carried loose in his pockets. It was brown wool, too broad in the shoulders and polished at the elbows. As a child, Mara had believed it made him invulnerable. Rain couldn’t reach him in that coat. Cold couldn’t enter. Once, when a dog barked and lunged at them from behind a chain-link fence, he had opened one side of the coat and swept her into it. She remembered darkness, wool against her cheek, and the deep machinery of his breathing.

For eleven months the coat had hung in her hallway.

Then that afternoon, while searching its pockets, she found a stain near the cuff. Coffee, perhaps. Mud. Something ordinary and old. Without thinking, she carried the coat downstairs, took two buses to the only all-night laundromat she knew, and fed it into a machine.

Now she regretted it.

The washer churned with brutal efficiency. Through the glass, the coat appeared and vanished in gray water, its sleeves reaching upward, collapsing, reaching again.

“You’re not supposed to wash wool like that.”

Mara looked up.

A boy stood beside the vending machine. Seventeen, perhaps younger. He wore red sneakers and a white shirt with a name tag that said RON, though there were no employees at this hour.

“I know,” Mara said.

He nodded, accepting this. “Then why’d you do it?”

“I don’t know.”

The boy put three coins into the machine and selected crackers. The metal spiral turned, but the package caught at the edge and hung there.

“Figures,” he said.

He shook the machine gently, then with conviction.

“You’re not supposed to do that,” Mara said.

“I know.”

“Then why are you doing it?”

He glanced at her, and for half a second his face remained solemn. Then he laughed. Mara laughed too—unexpectedly, almost angrily—and the sound startled them both.

The crackers fell.

Ron sat three chairs away and opened the package. “You want one?”

“No, thank you.”

He ate in silence, looking out at the traffic lights.

Red. Green. Yellow.

“Those things must get lonely,” he said.

“They have each other.”

“They’re all looking different directions.”

“Maybe that helps.”

The boy considered this. “Maybe.”

Mara closed her book. “Is your name Ron?”

“No. Found the shirt at a bus stop.”

“What’s your name?”

“Elias.”

“What are you washing?”

He pointed to a machine at the far end. Inside it, one pair of jeans and two black socks tumbled in an extravagant amount of foam.

“That’s all?”

“It’s what I’ve got dirty.”

Mara wanted to ask where he lived, why he was awake, why he had found or taken a shirt from a bus stop and decided to wear it. But she knew how questions could become doors, and how not everyone wanted a door opened.

The coat’s washer entered its final spin. It clung to the drum as if pinned by a great invisible hand.

“When my mom died,” Elias said, still watching the street, “I kept a message she left on my phone. Just saying she was at the grocery store and asking if we needed milk. I listened to it so much that I stopped hearing her voice. It became noises.”

Mara looked at him.

“I deleted it,” he continued. “By accident. Sort of.”

“Sort of?”

“I was afraid if I kept listening, there’d be nothing left of her in it.”

The washer slowed.

Mara stood and opened the door. The coat came out heavy and shrunken, darker than before. Water streamed from its sleeves onto the tiled floor. It no longer smelled of cigarettes or cedar or peppermint. It smelled of detergent named Alpine Morning.

She pressed her face into it anyway.

For a moment there was nothing. Then—not a scent, not a voice, but something quieter—she remembered her father standing at the kitchen counter, peeling an orange with a little knife. He had removed the skin in one unbroken spiral. He held it up proudly, and she applauded.

The memory was so clear that it hurt.

Then it was gone.

“Ruined?” Elias asked.

Mara lowered the coat. “Yes.”

“Sorry.”

“It’s all right.”

Outside, the rain had stopped. Water shone on the avenue, gathering the red light, then the green, then the yellow, without keeping any of them.

Mara placed the coat in a dryer and chose low heat.

Elias lifted his two socks and one pair of jeans from their machine. Together they waited for morning, while the city practiced changing its mind.
